Adult specimens of the Brick soldierfish (Myripristis amaena) exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 26.5 centimeters [Li = 26.5 centimeters], a size consistent with other members of the Holocentridae family that inhabit coral reef environments. Growth to this ultimate length proceeds through a juvenile phase characterized by rapid somatic development, during which individuals attain a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters] at the onset of puberty. Field studies conducted in the warm waters of the Indo-Pacific have demonstrated that sexual maturation is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, with the transition to reproductive capability typically occurring once this morphological threshold is crossed. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this length at first maturation is near the median for the genus, reflecting an intermediate life-history strategy that balances early maturation against the advantages of continued somatic growth. The ecological pressures exerted by predation on smaller individuals may have favored the evolution of a moderately large size at first maturation among these nocturnal planktivores, as a larger body provides both improved foraging efficiency on zooplankton and a reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the embryonic development of Brick soldierfish proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after an incubation period of just 3.6 days [ab = 3.6 days]. This short developmental interval is characteristic of tropical marine fishes with small, pelagic eggs, as the elevated thermal regime accelerates metabolic processes during the cleavage and gastrulation stages. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are exceptionally small, possessing a wet weight of only 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] immediately following eclosion. This minimal body mass at birth reflects the tiny egg diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters from which they hatch, a dimension that facilitates high fecundity at the cost of reduced per-offspring investment. The endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching, a period during which they remain non-feeding and vulnerable to planktonic predators. The rapid transition from chorion rupture to the onset of exogenous feeding is critical for survival in the oligotrophic waters these fish inhabit.

Reproductive output in Myripristis amaena has been quantified through spawning observations conducted at a consistent ambient temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C]. Gravid females produce an average of 600,000 eggs per annual spawning season [Ri = 600,000 eggs per annual spawning season], and because each female typically completes a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], the total yearly fecundity reaches this substantial figure. This extraordinary fecundity is typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts that release small, buoyant eggs into the water column, where the probability of any individual offspring surviving to recruitment is exceedingly low. The maximum reproductive rate, achieved when females are at their peak body condition of approximately 225 grams, reflects the energetic constraints of converting somatic reserves into gametic biomass. The high numerical output represents an evolved compensatory strategy against the immense mortality experienced during the early planktonic life stages, a common pattern among coral-reef fishes whose larvae face intense predation and stochastic oceanographic transport.

Juvenile individuals undergo a protracted growth period before reaching the body mass characteristic of mature adults. The wet weight at puberty is approximately 88 grams [Wwp = approximately 88 grams], a relatively modest mass compared to the asymptotic adult value, suggesting that reproductive investment begins well before somatic growth is complete. This mass at maturation is considerably lower than the asymptotic mass attained by fully grown adults, which reaches an ultimate wet weight of 505 grams [Wwi = 505 grams]. The disparity between these two mass values underscores a life-history pattern in which reproductive activity commences well before somatic growth is complete, a strategy that allows individuals to begin contributing to the next generation while still increasing their body size and competitive ability. Continued growth beyond puberty is supported by the abundant zooplankton resources available in their reef habitat, enabling females to eventually achieve the larger body sizes that are correlated with higher per-spawn fecundity. The length-mass relationship for this species, modeled with an exponent near 3.08, indicates a slightly positively allometric growth form, which may explain the disproportionally large mass gain relative to length increases after maturation.

Longevity records for Brick soldierfish indicate a maximum lifespan of 5500 days [am = 5500 days] when maintained under the stable thermal conditions typical of their natural habitat at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C]. This remarkable longevity, equivalent to approximately 15 years, places Myripristis amaena among the longer-lived members of its family, a trait that may be linked to its relatively slow pace of life and the protective refuge offered by daytime sheltering in crevices and caves. The extended lifespan of 5500 days allows for multiple reproductive seasons over a female's lifetime, a classic iteroparous pattern that spreads the risk of reproductive failure across years. Senescence in this species likely manifests as a gradual decline in spawning success and a reduction in condition factor during the final years of life. Comparative physiological studies suggest that the sustained low metabolic demands of a planktivorous diet, combined with the absence of intense physical activity outside of nocturnal foraging bouts, contribute to this species' capacity for long-term survival in a thermally stable environment.
